name: Jade Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now, in November, it's mostly the sprayer and walking fields. I'm out at seven checking the winter wheat for slugs and weeds, with a weed app on my phone that tells me what I'm looking at, because I'm still not great at telling blackgrass from wheat when they're tiny. Then it's the sprayer for a few hours, and in the afternoon I'm in the office with Graham, the farm manager, going over the yield maps from harvest. I love the maps, honestly, seeing the whole year in colours. What wears me out is the long days at harvest, sixteen hours in the combine cab, and the feeling that the people who own the land never see any of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who owns the farm, and how did you end up there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's the Wexcombe Estate, 850 hectares of wheat, barley, oilseed rape and beans, and it's owned by an investment company in the city. I'd never heard of them until I saw the logo on a letter. I grew up in town and only got into farming at twenty-one, driving a grain trailer for a summer, and I just stayed. So I'm four years behind people who grew up on farms, and I know it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Sam, who's an electrician, in a rented place near the estate. My dad died when I was nineteen and left me some money, and I put most of it into index funds, which are big bundles of shares, so it just sits and grows. I use AI tools every day, for spray rules, for drafting emails to the agronomist, for working out costs per field. Graham calls me the robot, which is half a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? A bit disappointing. I've kind of bet on it being useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, just not magic. It saves me an hour a day on paperwork and helps me spot weeds, and that's real. I'd probably post something like, the boring version of the future is still a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit relieved for people like Keith, our combine driver. But I'd also be annoyed, because I was hoping the tools would close the gap between me and people who grew up on farms. Without that, I'm just someone who started late and has to catch up the slow way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I've got and get my licence to fly a spray drone next spring, which costs about two thousand. Then I'd offer drone crop scouting to the smaller farms around us on my days off. It's a few hundred a job, and they'd pay it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little disappointment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 'the slow way' of catching up look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walking fields with Graham every week for years, and getting things wrong. The old guys can smell a wet patch of field. I need an app and a map to tell me what they just know. Without the shortcut, I just have to grow that nose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be glad for, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keith, definitely. He's been driving combines here for thirty years and he can't stand screens. In this picture he just retires when he wants to, not when a machine decides.

S0.say: I'd say AI is still useful, just not magic, because it saves me an hour of paperwork a day and helps me spot weeds. I'd post that the boring version of the future is still a future.
S0.think: I think I'd be relieved for older colleagues, but annoyed for myself, because I hoped the tools would close my gap with people who grew up on farms. Without them, I just catch up the slow way.
S0.do: Keeps using the AI tools she has and gets a spray drone licence next spring for about two thousand. Offers drone crop scouting to smaller neighbouring farms on her days off.
S0.feel: Calm, with a touch of disappointment.
S0.quote: The old guys can smell a wet patch of field. I need an app and a map to tell me what they just know.
S0.fieldNote: She's the rare farmer who is mildly let down by the quiet picture, because she sees AI as her way to catch up after starting late. Even so, she thought first of the older combine driver and was glad for him. Her side business idea came instantly, which suggests it's already in her head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one excites me, I'll be honest. And it also makes me feel a bit guilty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance to make farming less brutal, fewer sixteen-hour days and fewer injuries, but only if the gains are shared. If the investment company saves money on wages, some of that should go back to workers and the village, not just to the shareholders. I'd post that, and I'd go to the meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm well placed in this one, because I'm already the one who runs the screens. Keith's not, and he's been here thirty years. So the same change that helps me pushes him out, and I don't love being on that side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the drone licence this winter and ask Graham to trial a self-driving tractor for cultivation next autumn, with me running it. I'd join one of the farmers' groups that pools field data so small farms get the same tools as the big ones. And I'd keep the drone scouting going on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit excited, and a bit guilty about Keith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Keith if he asked you about the tractor trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the truth, that I asked for it. Then I'd ask him to sit in the cab with me for the first week, because he knows every wet corner of every field. The robot's got my phone and Keith's memory. Without him it would drive straight into the pond on Field Nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're still learning. What's the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reading the crop. Knowing a field is hungry for nitrogen just by the colour, or that the rape's about to fall over. The tools give me numbers, but I don't always know what to do with them yet.

S1.say: I'd say this is a chance to make farming less brutal, with fewer long days and injuries, if the gains are shared. Savings on wages should partly go back to workers and the village, not just shareholders.
S1.think: I think I'm well placed because I already run the screens, while a colleague with thirty years here is not. The same change that helps me pushes him out, and I don't like being on that side.
S1.do: Gets the drone licence this winter and asks the farm manager to trial a self-driving tractor next autumn with her running it. Joins a farmers' group that pools field data for small farms and keeps her drone scouting going.
S1.feel: Mostly calm and a little excited, with guilt about her older colleague.
S1.quote: The robot's got my phone and Keith's memory. Without him it would drive straight into the pond on Field Nine.
S1.fieldNote: She moves first and knows it, and the guilt about her older colleague was real rather than polite. Her plan to put him in the cab with her blends her progressive instincts with her early-adopter habits. She is honest that the tools give her numbers she can't always read yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's not change, that's a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the public needs a share of what this produces, straight away, like a dividend paid to everyone. If a few companies own the machines that do all the work, we have to tax that and share it, or it's going to be ugly. I'd be posting that every day and going to campaign meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my whole advantage disappears. Being good with the tools only matters while the tools need a person. And the investment company that owns Wexcombe needs nobody at all, not me, not Graham, not Keith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the next year I'd join a campaign group pushing for a public dividend and go knocking on doors for it. I'd keep my money invested, but I'd move some of it into a community land trust, where a village buys land together so it isn't all owned by funds. After it arrives, I'd look for any work helping farms through the switch, but I'd expect that to last months, not years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I've got money, but anxious for everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, being early stops being an advantage. Everyone's an early adopter when the change is forced on them in two years. There's no time to build anything, only to grab something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want companies taxed and shared, but your savings are in shares. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't, really. My index funds would probably go up the same week my job disappears. I'd give a chunk of that to the land trust, but I know that's me trying to feel less like a hypocrite.

S2.say: I'd say the public needs a share of what this produces straight away, like a dividend paid to everyone. If a few companies own the machines, we must tax and share it, and I'd post and campaign for that daily.
S2.think: I think my advantage disappears, because being good with tools only matters while the tools need a person. The investment company that owns the farm would need nobody at all.
S2.do: Joins a campaign group for a public dividend and knocks on doors for it in the next year. Moves part of her investments into a community land trust and, after it arrives, looks for short-term work helping farms switch over.
S2.feel: Anxious, mostly for other people, since her own savings give her a cushion.
S2.quote: Everyone's an early adopter when the change is forced on them in two years.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture flips her early-adopter edge into nothing, and she saw that immediately. She was candid about the contradiction of holding shares while wanting companies taxed, and offered the land trust as part repair. Her worry is directed at the owners of the land and the machines, not at the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to actually do something clever, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to decide who owns this, so let's decide now. I'd push for public training money and for community ownership of farmland, so the robots work for villages, not funds. I'd say that at work, online, at the pub, anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd jump into the companies putting robots on farms, as the person who explains them to farmers. I know farmers and I know the tools, which is rare right now. It wouldn't last past 2031, but it'd be three or four good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to one of the farm robot companies in the first year, as a field trainer or support person. I'd keep the drone business on weekends and keep putting money into the land trust. And I'd ask Graham to let me run the robot trials at Wexcombe before I leave, so I've got something to show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly busy. Busy is good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me build a bit of a career out of the change itself. With two years, I grab what's there. With five, I can be the person farmers call when the robot's stuck in a hedge, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you take with you, if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Graham, if he wanted. Graham's spent twenty years learning that land, and I'd want the robot company to pay him for every year of it. Keith wouldn't come. He'd say he's too old, and he'd mean too proud.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years to decide who owns this, so decide now. I'd push for public training money and community ownership of farmland, and say it at work, online and at the pub.
S3.think: I think I'd move to a farm robot company as the person who explains the robots to farmers, since knowing both is rare. It wouldn't last past 2031, but it would give three or four good years.
S3.do: Applies to a farm robot company in the first year as a field trainer or support worker. Keeps the drone business at weekends, keeps funding the land trust and asks to run robot trials at the estate before leaving.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, and busy suits her.
S3.quote: Graham's spent twenty years learning that land, and I'd want the robot company to pay him for every year of it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns the change into a short career for her, and she is clear-eyed that it's temporary. She still thinks about colleagues, wanting her manager's experience paid for and reading her older colleague's refusal as pride. Her politics stay constant: ownership of land and machines is the real question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's plenty of time to change what I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan this like grown-ups. Public training, community land, a share of the profits for everyone. I'd say it loudly, and I'd probably stand for the parish council, which I've never thought about before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd stop trying to be the best robot driver and go for the bit that decides how land is used. Soil, water, what gets grown where. Somebody still has to choose what a field is for, even if a robot does the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time degree in soil and land management in the first year, three or four years of evening and online study. I'd keep the drone business and run the robot trials at Wexcombe in the meantime. And I'd help our village set up the land trust properly, with my money and my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. It's the one where I get to steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years change, compared with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five, I ride the wave. With ten, I can stop being the one who drives the robot and become the one who decides what the field is for. That's a different job and a better one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sam say about you doing a degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say about time. He's always said I'm wasted on the sprayer. He'd also say I'll be unbearable at dinner, talking about soil, and he's right.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to plan this like grown-ups, with public training, community land and a share of the profits for everyone. I'd probably stand for the parish council.
S4.think: I think I'd stop trying to be the best robot operator and move into deciding how land is used, like soil, water and what grows where. Someone still has to choose what a field is for.
S4.do: Starts a part-time degree in soil and land management in the first year. Keeps the drone business, runs robot trials on the estate and helps the village set up the land trust with money and time.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more excited than scared, because she gets to steer.
S4.quote: With ten, I can stop being the one who drives the robot and become the one who decides what the field is for.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years moves her from using the tools to deciding what the land is for, a jump she'd clearly been building up to. It was the first time she mentioned stepping into local politics herself, through the parish council. Her partner appears as a steady, joking supporter in the background of her plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not mostly for me, I'd land somewhere. For Keith, and for the village, and for everyone who doesn't have a dad's money sitting in funds. What would help is a public share in what the robots earn, paid to everyone, and money for people to retrain without having to quit their jobs first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the land. That's the question under all of this. If farms are owned by funds in the city, the robots just make the city richer.

headlineQuote: My index funds would probably go up the same week my job disappears.
portrait: Jade Kowalski is 27, came into farming late at 21, and is a junior on an 850-hectare grain and oilseed estate owned by an investment company. She uses AI tools every day, has an inheritance invested in index funds, and lives with her electrician partner Sam. She sees AI as her way to catch up with people who grew up on farms, while feeling guilty about older colleagues it could push out. In AI Plateau and Steady Disruption she builds a drone side business and runs robot trials, and in AGI by 2028 she turns to campaigning for a public dividend and a community land trust. With five years she'd ride the change as a robot trainer, and with ten she'd study land management to decide what fields are for.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, mainly for her older colleague, her village and people without savings, rather than for herself.
whatWouldHelp: A public share of what the robots earn, paid to everyone, and money for people to retrain without first quitting their jobs.
